Parameters ╭───────────┬──────────┬──────────┬──────────┬──────────┬────────────────────┬──────────────────╮ │ Parameter │ Type │ Required │ Position │ Pipeline │ Default │ Description │ ├───────────┼──────────┼──────────┼──────────┼──────────┼────────────────────┼──────────────────┤ │ -Domain │ String │ yes │ 1 │ ByValue │ │ The domain to │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ check, for │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ example │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ evotec.xyz. │ │ -Selector │ String[] │ no │ 2 │ no │ @('selector1') │ The DKIM │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ selectors to │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ look up. │ │ -Timeout │ TimeSpan │ no │ 3 │ no │ (New-TimeSpan │ How long to wait │ │ │ │ │ │ │ -Seconds 5) │ for each DNS │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ answer. │ ╰───────────┴──────────┴──────────┴──────────┴──────────┴────────────────────┴──────────────────╯ Common parameters: -Debug, -ErrorAction, -ErrorVariable, -InformationAction, -OutVariable, -Verbose, -WarningAction and the others (about_CommonParameters). help.powershellFull:
Import-Module ConsoleMonster

# Show-ConsoleHelp reads the help PowerShell already has: here a function's comment-based help.
function Test-MailDomain {
    <#
    .SYNOPSIS
    Checks the mail records of a domain: MX, SPF, DMARC, DKIM and MTA-STS.

    .DESCRIPTION
    Resolves each record, compares it with the recommended settings and returns one result per check.

    .PARAMETER Domain
    The domain to check, for example evotec.xyz.

    .PARAMETER Selector
    The DKIM selectors to look up.

    .PARAMETER Timeout
    How long to wait for each DNS answer.

    .EXAMPLE
    Test-MailDomain -Domain evotec.xyz

    .EXAMPLE
    'evotec.xyz', 'evotec.pl' | Test-MailDomain -Selector selector1, selector2 | Show-ConsoleTable
    #>
    [CmdletBinding()]
    param(
        [Parameter(Mandatory, ValueFromPipeline)][string] $Domain,
        [string[]] $Selector = @('selector1'),
        [timespan] $Timeout = (New-TimeSpan -Seconds 5)
    )
    process { [pscustomobject] @{ Domain = $Domain; Checks = 5 } }
}

Show-ConsoleHelp Test-MailDomain

progress.powershell:
# An ordinary Write-Progress loop, drawn by ConsoleMonster once the Progress feature is on.
Enable-ConsoleFormatting -Feature Progress
$sites = 'Warsaw', 'Dublin', 'Berlin'
for ($i = 0; $i -lt $sites.Count; $i++) {
    $progressParameters = @{
        Id = 1
        Activity = 'Collecting inventory'
        Status = $sites[$i]
        PercentComplete = ($i * 100 / $sites.Count)
    }
    Write-Progress @progressParameters
    foreach ($server in 1..12) {
        $progressParameters = @{
            Id = 2
            ParentId = 1
            Activity = "Servers in $($sites[$i])"
            Status = "SRV$server"
            PercentComplete = ($server * 100 / 12)
        }
        Write-Progress @progressParameters
        Start-Sleep -Milliseconds 110
    }
    Write-Host "$($sites[$i]) done: 12 servers"
}
Write-Progress -Id 2 -Activity 'Servers' -Completed
Write-Progress -Id 1 -Activity 'Collecting inventory' -Completed

hosting.powershellFull:
<#
.SYNOPSIS
Runs the .NET integration project from PowerShell.
.DESCRIPTION
Create the project and save Program.cs from either C# tab first. The .NET host and logging provider own this lifecycle;
there is no separate PowerShell hosting implementation.
.PARAMETER Project
The project file or directory containing the saved C# program (default current directory).
#>
[CmdletBinding()]
param([string] $Project = '.')

& dotnet run --project $Project -c Release
if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw "The .NET example exited with code $LASTEXITCODE." }
hosting.powershellNote: PowerShell launches the same .NET project after Program.cs is saved from either C# tab. The generic host and ILogger provider have no separate cmdlet implementation.

apiMap.note: The .NET generic host owns service discovery, worker lifetimes and shutdown; PowerShell dashboard scripts use Invoke-ConsoleDashboard instead.

The .NET logging provider is configured through its logging builder; PowerShell launches the same project with dotnet.
